title: How To Be A Great Teacher Through Modeling In The Classroom
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes the case that modeling is the single most powerful tool for teaching classroom management, more effective and memorable than verbal instruction alone. He lays out eleven guidelines for doing it well: modeling every routine, knowing exactly what is wanted before starting, physically acting as one of the students rather than narrating from the front, being highly detailed, adding small insignificant anchor details, speaking sparingly, chaining several routines together into a longer sequence, having students follow along physically, using student helpers when needed, allowing supervised practice, and closely observing and correcting errors. He argues that this level of precision in modeling produces both excellent classroom management and great teaching overall.
points: Modeling is presented as more powerful and memorable than verbal instruction for teaching classroom routines and expectations.
Effective modeling requires physically acting as a student — sitting at a desk, wearing a backpack — rather than narrating expectations from the front of the room.
Adding small, seemingly insignificant details to a modeled routine acts as memory 'anchors' that help students recall the full sequence.
Modeling should be accompanied by minimal verbal explanation, since physical demonstration should do most of the communicating.
Chaining several routines together into one longer modeled sequence, rather than modeling only one thing at a time, improves retention.
quotes: Because showing students what you expect is infinitely more powerful, more meaningful, and more memorable than voice instruction will ever be—by a long shot.
When you model, don’t stand in the front of your classroom trying to mimic what you want your students to do. Instead, show them what you expect by actually doing it—as if you’re one of them.

These extra details, which can be as simple and insignificant as tapping a poster on the way into the classroom or as silly as dancing a jig after turning in work, act as anchors along the memory map you’re constructing for your students.
Your physical movements and actions should do most of the talking for you. Instructions only support your modeling.
Asking your students for the moon and then modeling for them exactly—precisely—how to get it, is a recipe for not only excellent classroom management, but for great teaching as well.
